policy.why: Automatic T1 used to be limited to government suffixes, so go.dev, kubernetes.io and rfc-editor.org all derived as T4 and no High-confidence single fact about Go, Kubernetes or an RFC was reachable. Shape-based rules cannot fix that without reopening the self-declared-official hole: any host can be named docs.something. This registry is the middle path — a small, curated, versioned list where each entry records who owns the domain and when that was checked.

authority_levels.standards-body: Publishes the normative text of a standard. T1 for any claim about that standard.
authority_levels.project-owned: The domain is operated by the project that produces the software. T1 for a narrow factual claim about that project's own behavior, API or configuration. NOT an independent source: for comparisons, benchmarks and recommendations it is vendor-self evidence and cannot serve as the primary leg of a two-independent-source High.

limits: Registry membership proves domain ownership, never correctness. A project's own documentation can be stale or wrong.
Subject fields document why the entry exists and are surfaced in the classification basis. The executable rule binds authority to the domain, not to a per-finding subject declaration.
An unlisted domain keeps its heuristic classification. Absence from this file is never evidence that a source is untrustworthy.
Entries must be re-checked when verified_on is older than a year.
